lead: A stereo FM station must send two audio signals, left and right, through one 200 kHz channel. It does this by building a composite baseband: the sum L + R in the ordinary audio band so old mono radios still work, a small 19 kHz pilot tone, and the difference L − R on a suppressed 38 kHz subcarrier. The receiver recovers the carrier from the pilot, detects the difference, and matrixes sum and difference back into left and right. The same idea runs in every FM stereo chip and in software-defined radio.
prereq: You need: the discriminator from Chapter 3.4, de-emphasis from Chapter 3.7, and the superheterodyne front end with its 10.7 MHz IF from Unit 2.

blocks.text: One carrier, one 200 kHz channel, two audio signals. Sending left (L) and right (R) on two separate carriers would waste spectrum, so the transmitter combines them into one audio-frequency signal called the composite baseband and modulates the carrier with it. Stereo FM is frequency-division multiplexing applied to FM (see Unit 2, Frequency division multiplexing).

Compatibility drives the layout. A mono receiver tuned to a stereo station must still sound right. So the transmitter forms the sum L + R and puts it in the plain audio band, 0 to 15 kHz. A mono receiver low-pass filters the discriminator output at 15 kHz and hears L + R, which for a listener between the speakers is the whole programme. Nothing is lost.

The difference L − R carries the stereo information and needs its own band, placed above the audio. It modulates a 38 kHz subcarrier with both sidebands and no carrier, so it occupies (38 − 15) = 23 kHz to (38 + 15) = 53 kHz. That 30 kHz block is empty when L = R, since the difference is then zero. Anything above 53 kHz, such as a 67 kHz subsidiary channel, is optional extra.

blocks.where: L and R are the left and right audio voltages; (L + R) comes from the 0–15 kHz band and (L − R) from the synchronous detector. This adding and subtracting is the matrix.

blocks.text: The difference channel is double-sideband suppressed-carrier. Suppressing the carrier saves nearly all the transmitted power, but coherent detection needs a reference at exactly 38 kHz with the right phase. So the transmitter sends a small unmodulated tone at half that frequency, 19 kHz, called the pilot. It sits in the empty gap between 15 kHz audio and the 23 kHz lower edge of the difference channel, where it interferes with nothing and costs little: about 8 to 10 percent of the total deviation.

The receiver doubles the pilot to get 38 kHz. A frequency doubler or a phase-locked loop does this exactly: 2 × 19 kHz = 38 kHz, and the output phase is locked to the pilot. The transmitter's own subcarrier was produced by doubling the same 19 kHz oscillator, so the receiver's locally generated 38 kHz stays phase-coherent with the suppressed carrier. That is the whole reason the pilot is at half the subcarrier frequency and not at 38 kHz itself.
Phase matters. If the recovered 38 kHz is off by an angle φ, the synchronous detector scales the wanted difference by cos φ and leaks some of the sum channel into it.

blocks.where: S is the left-right separation in dB and φ is the pilot phase error in radians. φ = 10° gives cot φ = 5.67 and S ≈ 15 dB, poor; φ = 1° gives about 35 dB, acceptable.

blocks.text: FM broadcasting uses 88 to 108 MHz with channels spaced 200 kHz apart, so a station's deviation of 75 kHz and its sidebands fit with room to spare. The receiver is a superheterodyne, and every stage has a job.

items: Antenna picks up 88–108 MHz and the RF amplifier selects the wanted channel and sets the noise figure.
The mixer with a local oscillator at f_LO = f_c + 10.7 MHz shifts the channel down to the intermediate frequency of 10.7 MHz.
The IF amplifier, with a filter about 200 kHz wide, provides most of the gain and the selectivity.
The limiter strips amplitude variations, so noise that arrived as AM never reaches the detector.
The discriminator converts frequency deviation into voltage, giving back the composite baseband.
The stereo decoder runs: a narrow 19 kHz pilot filter, a doubler, a synchronous detector for L − R, and a matrix.

De-emphasis and low-pass filtering on each output cut the treble that pre-emphasis boosted, restoring flat audio response and, at the same time, cutting much of the high-frequency noise picked up in transmission.
Two audio power amplifiers drive the loudspeakers.

blocks.text: De-emphasis must be applied to baseband signals. Because de-emphasis and the matrix are both linear, putting one de-emphasis network on each output after the matrix gives the same result as putting one network on L + R and one on L − R after detection but before the matrix. It is not equivalent to filtering the composite. A mono receiver skips the decoder entirely and applies de-emphasis to L + R.

figure.caption: The sum takes the low band, the difference rides a suppressed 38 kHz subcarrier from 23 to 53 kHz, and the 19 kHz pilot sits between them to lock the receiver's subcarrier.

spec.title: FM stereo transmitter
spec.aria: Left and right are added and subtracted; the sum stays in the baseband, the difference rides a suppressed 38 kHz subcarrier, a 19 kHz pilot is added, and the three parts form the composite signal fed to the FM modulator.

examples.question: A stereo FM transmitter is fed test tones of L = 1 V and R = 0.5 V peak. Find the matrix outputs, the frequency bands present in the composite signal, the total composite bandwidth, and the signals the receiver recovers after the matrix.
steps: The sum occupies the audio band 0 to 15 kHz. A mono receiver hears only this.
The difference is DSB-SC on 38 kHz, so its sidebands span 38 − 15 = 23 kHz to 38 + 15 = 53 kHz.
The pilot is added at 19 kHz, in the gap between 15 kHz and 23 kHz. Total composite bandwidth = 53 kHz.
The receiver filters the pilot, doubles 19 kHz to 38 kHz, and synchronously detects, recovering L − R = 0.5 V.
Matrix: L = (1.5 + 0.5)/2 = 1.0 V and R = (1.5 − 0.5)/2 = 0.5 V, matching the inputs.
examples.answer: L + R = 1.5 V, L − R = 0.5 V, composite bands 0–15 kHz, 19 kHz pilot and 23–53 kHz, total bandwidth 53 kHz, and the receiver recovers L = 1.0 V and R = 0.5 V.

L = 1.0
R = 0.5
s = L + R
d = L - R
print(s)
print(d)
print(38 - 15)
print(38 + 15)
print((s + d) / 2)
print((s - d) / 2)

traps: Pilot is 19 kHz and the subcarrier is 38 kHz. Writing it the other way round is the commonest mistake; the subcarrier itself is suppressed and never transmitted.
The difference channel is DSB-SC, not SSB and not FM. It needs both sidebands, 23 to 53 kHz, so the composite is 53 kHz wide.
A mono receiver loses nothing. It hears L + R, which is the full mono programme; its 15 kHz low-pass removes the pilot and the difference channel.
A phase error in the doubled pilot leaks the sum into the difference. Amplitude error only changes level; phase error destroys separation.
The pilot and the difference channel share the 75 kHz deviation. They do not sit outside it, and the 200 kHz channel spacing is set by Carson's rule plus guard band.

quiz.q: State the pilot frequency, the subcarrier frequency, and the band occupied by the difference channel.
quiz.a: Pilot 19 kHz; subcarrier 38 kHz suppressed; difference channel 23 kHz to 53 kHz.

quiz.q: Why is the difference sent as DSB-SC instead of ordinary DSB with a carrier?
quiz.a: A transmitted 38 kHz carrier would use up most of the power in the difference channel while carrying no information, and the receiver would need extra filtering to keep it from biasing the difference detector. Suppressing it and sending a small 19 kHz pilot is far cheaper in power, and the pilot is doubled back to 38 kHz with the correct phase.

quiz.q: A stereo signal has L = 0.8 V and R = 0.2 V. Find the matrix outputs and the occupied bands in the composite.
quiz.a: L + R = 1.0 V in 0–15 kHz; L − R = 0.6 V on 38 kHz, spanning 23–53 kHz; pilot at 19 kHz. Total bandwidth 53 kHz.

quiz.q: The recovered subcarrier in a stereo decoder has a phase error of 10°. Estimate the separation in dB.
quiz.a: cot 10° = 5.67, so S = 20 log₁₀ 5.67 = 15.1 dB. That is far below the 30 dB or more a good decoder needs.

quiz.q: Why must the pilot be exactly half the subcarrier frequency rather than an unrelated reference tone?
quiz.a: The receiver makes the subcarrier by doubling the pilot. Doubling gives 2 × 19 = 38 kHz and locks the phase to the pilot. If the pilot were at any other frequency, doubling would not land on 38 kHz and the synchronous detector would have the wrong frequency and phase, so the difference channel would not be recovered.

quiz.q: A listener says a stereo station sounds correct on an old mono radio but the stereo light never comes on. Explain.
quiz.a: The mono radio low-pass filters at 15 kHz and reproduces L + R, the full mono programme. It has no pilot filter, no doubler and no decoder, so it never regenerates the 38 kHz subcarrier or extracts L − R. The stereo indication is missing because the difference channel is simply discarded.

quiz.q: Give the FM broadcast band, the channel spacing, and the intermediate frequency of an FM receiver.
quiz.a: 88–108 MHz, 200 kHz channel spacing, 10.7 MHz IF.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real receivers add a 57 kHz subcarrier carrying RDS data, which is itself locked to the third harmonic of the pilot, and that is how a car radio shows the station name. Digital systems such as HD Radio and DAB+ carry the audio in coded form but keep the same idea of a multiplexed baseband. Modern stereo decoders are often a few lines of DSP code inside a software-defined radio, doing the pilot recovery with a phase-locked loop. Useful search terms: FM composite baseband, pilot-tone stereo decoder, RDS 57 kHz, and stereo separation measurement.
